Studies have shown that minoxidil is effective in stabilizing hair loss in 60 to 80% of users, with approximately 30% reporting cosmetically satisfactory results [0]. In summary, minoxidil is a clinically supported treatment for hair loss that can stabilize hair loss and promote regrowth, particularly in early-stage androgenetic alopecia and on the crown of the scalp [2, 3]. Therefore, while minoxidil can be a useful tool in managing hair loss, it is not a permanent solution and should be considered as part of a broader treatment strategy that may include addressing hormonal imbalances or other contributing factors [1, 4].

description: Can folic acid help improve cognition and treat dementia?
llm_response: Folic acid may help improve cognition, particularly in individuals with elevated homocysteine levels or low baseline folate status, but its effectiveness in treating dementia remains uncertain and context-dependent. Several studies indicate that folic acid supplementation can reduce homocysteine levels, which are associated with cognitive decline and increased risk of Alzheimer’s disease [3]. For instance, a randomized, double-blind, controlled trial involving 818 older adults with raised homocysteine levels and normal vitamin B12 levels found that those receiving 800 micrograms of folic acid daily for three years showed lower homocysteine levels and improved cognitive performance compared to the placebo group [1]. Similarly, a study of men aged 50–85 in the Boston-area Normative Aging Study demonstrated that higher dietary folate intake was associated with significantly less decline in verbal fluency and spatial copying skills over three years, independent of homocysteine levels [1]. Furthermore, data from the Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging revealed that individuals consuming 400 micrograms or more of folic acid daily had a 55% reduction in the risk of developing Alzheimer’s disease over a follow-up period of up to 14 years [7]. However, the evidence for folic acid’s benefits in dementia treatment is less consistent. A preliminary report on 11 patients with dementia and low-normal folic acid levels found no significant cognitive improvement with folic acid supplementation (10 mg/day), and there was even a trend toward worsening performance on certain cognitive measures, although the study was limited by a small sample size and low completion rate [8]. Moreover, meta-analyses have yielded equivocal results. One analysis of 19 studies involving older adults found no evidence that folic acid, with or without vitamins B12 and B6, improved or attenuated cognitive decline, regardless of baseline cognitive status or study duration [9]. Another meta-analysis of 11 studies involving over 22,000 participants similarly found no significant benefits on global cognitive function or specific cognitive domains, despite substantial reductions in homocysteine levels [9]. These null findings may be influenced by methodological factors such as the cognitive status of participants at baseline, the duration of treatment, and the sensitivity of cognitive tests used [9]. Importantly, the benefits of folic acid may be more pronounced in specific subgroups. For example, B vitamin supplementation was found to be more effective in slowing cognitive decline in individuals with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) who also had high baseline levels of omega-3 fatty acids, particularly DHA [4]. Additionally, the protective effects of folic acid appear to depend on adequate vitamin B12 levels: seniors with normal B12 levels perform better when folate levels are high, but high folate levels in the presence of low B12 are associated with poor cognitive performance and increased anemia risk [1, 3]. This interaction underscores the importance of balanced B-vitamin status rather than isolated folic acid supplementation. In summary, while folic acid supplementation shows promise in improving cognition in older adults with elevated homocysteine or low folate levels, and may reduce the risk of Alzheimer’s disease, its efficacy in treating established dementia is not well-supported by current evidence [1, 7, 8, 9]. The inconsistent results across studies suggest that folic acid may be most beneficial as part of a broader nutritional strategy that includes adequate B12, omega-3 fatty acids, and overall dietary quality, rather than as a standalone treatment for dementia [4, 9]. Therefore, folic acid may play a preventive role in cognitive health but should not be considered a definitive treatment for dementia at this time.
